title: How To Connect With Students Who Don't Want To Connect
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin argues that pulling shy or distrustful students out of their shell backfires, making them retreat further, and offers instead a five-part method for drawing reluctant students in gradually and indirectly. The steps are: overlook their reticence entirely rather than drawing attention to it; pretend any participation attempt, however awkward, is completely normal; move on quickly from interactions so students don't have to linger outside their comfort zone; wait on the student's own timetable rather than the teacher's; and hearten them with ordinary praise once they've grown more comfortable, without becoming effusive. He estimates up to 40 percent of a class may be shy, and closes by noting the technique benefits every student, not just the shy ones, because it creates the freedom within boundaries that all students crave.

The five-step method: overlook reticence, pretend participation is normal, keep interactions brief, wait on the student's timetable, then hearten with ordinary praise.
Never lingering on a shy student's contribution avoids making them feel put on the spot.
Up to 40 percent of a class may be shy, according to the surveys Linsin cites.
The same laid-back, non-intrusive approach to rapport benefits every student, not just shy ones.
quotes: This is the mistake teachers make. Trying to pull quiet, shy, or distrustful students out of their shell does the opposite.
You must never speak, take notice of, or react in any way that highlights their reticence. Although counterintuitive, if they perceive you’re trying to draw them out, the jig is up.
No matter how awkward they appear, if ever they take a chance to participate, you must pretend that whatever they said or did was the most normal thing in the world.
All interactions between you and them must be quick hits, before they can begin to squirm too long outside their comfort zone.
Becoming an active participant in your classroom is on their timetable, not yours.
According to surveys, up to 40% of your class may be shy. They’re worth your understanding and adjustment to their needs.
